$note: A crash mid-batch is completed by the next attempt, and a duplicate delivery lands once (#1020, D-1020-D1-11). Hand-authored: the claim is about what happens BETWEEN two applies, which no row dump states.
$whyItIsOneGateAndNotTwo: Idempotence under duplicate delivery and recovery after a crash are the same property seen twice. An insert of a row already present is the upsert's no-op update; a delete of a row already gone deletes nothing. So a batch delivered twice lands the same state, and a batch half-delivered can simply be delivered again — which is why the applier needs no journal of its own, only a cursor that refuses to move backwards.

cases.name: a crash mid-batch is completed by the next attempt
cases.$how: Apply only the first commit's rows, then apply the WHOLE batch. The second attempt must land the rest and must not double-apply the first.

cases.name: duplicate delivery lands once
cases.$how: Apply the whole batch twice. The row set, every row's values and the cursor must be identical after the second apply.

cases.name: the applier is last-write-wins by DELIVERY order, and the cursor is what makes that safe
cases.$how: Apply the whole batch, then apply only the FIRST commit again. `atom-a` goes BACK to its original name, because the applier is a faithful mirror of the row image it was handed and does not second-guess it.
cases.$why: This is the honest statement of the property, and the temptation is to assert the opposite. An applier that compared `row_version` and refused an older image would need a version on every table — and 51 replicated tables have none (plane census seam 9), so it would silently refuse nothing on exactly those. What actually makes redelivery safe is that a SEAT NEVER ASKS FOR ROWS BELOW ITS CURSOR: the cursor refuses to move backwards (`record_seat_cursor`), the door refuses a cursor below the floor, and the log serves `seq > since`. The ordering guarantee lives in the door, not in the applier.
